feedback: If the learner counts 150, 250, 350 but drops the 50 to say 100, 200, 300, point to the five tens rods still sitting on the mat and ask what should have stayed the same.
If the learner recites a number but adds the wrong piece, map the spoken digit to the matching column of blocks before continuing.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding 10 or 100 physically adds a rod or a flat, and crossing a boundary is the concrete act of trading ten rods for one flat — making the digit that changes something the learner can handle and see, not just recite.
learnerActions: Build a start number with hundreds flats, tens rods and unit cubes (e.g. 190 as one flat and nine rods).
To add 10, physically add one tens rod; to add 100, add one hundreds flat — and say which digit changed.
At 190, add the tenth rod, then trade ten rods for one hundreds flat to make 200, and say 'the tens rolled to 0 and the hundreds went up by one'.
Skip-count by 100s from 150 using flats, keeping the five tens and nothing in the ones fixed, to reach 250, 350 … 950.
activities.title: Hands-on regrouping with base-ten materials

feedback: Expected: 150, 250 … 950; 480, 485 … 520 crossing 500 correctly; 1000, 990, 980 …; and 620, 720, 820, 920, 1020 crossing the thousand boundary cleanly. (985, __, 1005 fills to 995.)
'10 more than 268' = 278; if a learner offers 2680, that is the 'add a zero' error — show the tens digit rolling 6→7 instead. ('100 more than 613' = 713.)
If the learner snaps 100s-from-150 to 100, 200, 300, name the dropped 50 and re-run keeping tens and ones fixed.

If an error appears precisely at 495→500 or at 1000 while mid-run counting is fine, treat it as a boundary-bridge gap: rehearse just 490, 495, 500, 505 and 980, 990, 1000, 1010 on a number line, naming the regrouping — do not re-drill the whole sequence.
If backward counting breaks only at boundaries, practise short backward runs across each boundary as its own skill; do not assume backward fluency arrives with forward.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means changing only the relevant place and crossing hundred and thousand boundaries cleanly, from non-round starts and in both directions.
learnerActions: Order a set of 100s cards from 240 and fill blanks in sequences that cross a boundary, e.g. 985, __, 1005.
Answer '100 more than 613' and '10 more than 268', writing the single digit that changed.
Count on in 100s from 150 up to 950; count in 5s from 480 up to 520; count back in 10s from 1000; count on in 100s from 620 and say what happens when the count passes 1000 (920 → 1020).
Explain for each: which digit changed and which stayed the same.
activities.title: Checking and diagnostic skip-count tasks

feedback: If the learner supplies a wrong boundary number, pause and return to a number line or blocks to show the regrouping before resuming the count.
Reward a correct boundary supply by having the learner name the digit that changed.
activities.intendedInsight: Rehearsing the count aloud, especially at the deliberate hesitation at a boundary, builds oral fluency and the habit of naming the carry.
learnerActions: Take turns skip-counting aloud with a counting buddy, alternating each number in a 10s or 100s run.
When the buddy hesitates at 190 in a 10s run, supply the next number (200) and say which digits rolled.
Say each number clearly and, at boundaries, state what carried before moving on.
activities.title: Count-with-me partner rehearsal (spoken practice)
